verdicts.why: Having a fact fixed in the mind is stated flatly; the word takes no side on the knower or the thing known.
Firsthand acquaintance with a state or feeling is a plain report of experience, not an attitude toward it.
Perceiving something as familiar is a neutral act of recognition with no approval or contempt in it.
Knowing someone's nature or character describes the depth of acquaintance and says nothing about whether that character is good or bad.
Being able to tell two things apart is a bare capacity; the word carries no judgement of either thing.
Accepting someone's claim or authority is reported neutrally; the word neither endorses nor mocks the authority accepted.
This is an archaic, biblical euphemism, which is a matter of register and delicacy, not of approval or contempt toward the act or the partner.
In this sense the word states inexperience as a stage not yet passed through, without the dismissiveness of green or raw.
Of crops, young simply marks the stage at which they were gathered; it is a technical description with no attitude.
A school sports award is named plainly; the word conveys no view of the award or its holder.
One who lets property is named by function alone, with none of the contempt that a word like slumlord carries.
Talk in the sense of divulging information names the act without taking a side on it, unlike snitch or squeal which condemn the talker.
Delivering a lecture is a neutral description of an activity, carrying no view of the speaker or the content.
A person under experimental observation is named in clinical, procedural terms with no judgement of that person.
A subject of a nation is defined by the allegiance owed, a matter of fact about political status rather than an attitude toward it.
The grammatical subject is a technical term with no evaluative content at all.
What an artist chooses to depict is named neutrally; the word passes no judgement on the thing chosen.
The first term of a proposition is a technical term in logic and carries no attitude.
Coming into being or onto the scene is stated flatly, with no approval or dismissal of what appears.
Being published is a plain event; the word says nothing about the merit of what was issued.
Presenting oneself before a court or authority is a formal, procedural description with no attitude in it.
Appearing in a play or on stage names the performer's presence without judging the performance.
Making certain that something is done is a neutral description of care taken, with no view of the thing secured.
Giving someone a promise or firm word is a plain speech act; its earnestness is its meaning, not an attitude beyond it.
Going after something and carrying it back is a bare physical action with no judgement of the thing fetched.
